# Tobit Chapter 11 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 11 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_011_page_001.jpg

---

**1** They were approaching Kaserin, on the outskirts of Nineveh,

**2** when Raphael said to Tobias, "You know what condition your father was in when you left.

**3** Let's go ahead of Sarah and get the house ready before she arrives."

**4** The two of them pressed on ahead. "Take the gall with you," Raphael said. The dog trotted along behind them.

**5** Anna was sitting outside, watching the road, the way she always did.

**6** She saw him first. She jumped up and called to Tobit: "He's coming! Your son is coming — and the man who went with him!"

**7** Raphael pulled Tobias aside before he reached his father. "I want you to know — your father's eyes are going to open.

**8** Spread the fish gall on his eyes. It will work. It will dissolve the film that covers them, and he will see light again."

**9** Anna came running. She threw herself onto her son and held him and said, "I can see you, my boy — I can actually see you. Now I could die happy." She wept.

**10** Inside, Tobit heard the commotion, stumbled to his feet, and made his way out through the courtyard. Tobias came toward him,

**11** the gall ready in his hand. He breathed on it gently, and then — steadying his father — pressed it to his eyes. "Don't be afraid, Father."

**12** The moment the medicine touched his eyes, they stung. Tobit rubbed at the corners of his eyes with both hands, and the white film came away — peeling off in pieces.

**13** Tobit's eyes cleared. He saw his son. He grabbed him, held him, and wept. "I can see you," he said. "My son — the light of my eyes." And he began to praise God.

**14** "Blessed are you, O God," he said. "Blessed is your name, forever and ever. Blessed are all your holy angels.

**15** You struck me down, and then you had mercy on me. And now I am looking at my son Tobias with my own eyes." Tobias went inside, his heart full of joy, and told his father everything that had happened to him in Media.

**16** Then Tobit went out to meet his daughter-in-law at the gates of Nineveh. He was walking. He was praising God out loud. Everyone who saw him stopped and stared — they could not believe it. And Tobit told them all: God had been merciful to him.

**17** When he came to Sarah, he blessed her: "Welcome home, daughter. Blessed is the God who brought you here to us. Blessed is your father. Blessed is my son Tobias. And blessed are you, daughter. Come into your home now, with joy. Come in with blessing. Come in with joy. Come in, my daughter."

**18** That day, every Jewish family in Nineveh celebrated.

**19** Ahikar and Nadab, Tobit's kinsmen, came to share in his happiness. And the wedding feast of Tobias lasted seven days, full of joy, with gifts pouring in from all sides.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

Chapter 11 is the emotional payoff of the entire book. Every storytelling instinct says: do not rush this. The healing scene (vv. 10-13) is one of the most carefully paced moments in ancient narrative literature.

- **Verse 4**: The dog is back. PNEUMA notes that the dog was mentioned at departure (6:2) and return (11:4) — it bookmarks the entire journey. "Trotted along" keeps the detail light but present.
- **Verse 6**: Anna sees Tobias first. She has been the one watching every day; it is right that she spots him first. PNEUMA renders "Look — your son is coming" as "He's coming! Your son is coming" to capture the breathless excitement.
- **Verse 9**: Anna's "now I can die" — this is the nunc dimittis of a mother. PNEUMA makes the emotion explicit: "now I could die happy." The Greek simply says "from now on I can die" but the implication is relief and fulfillment, not despair.
- **Verses 10-12**: The healing is rendered step by step. Every detail matters: Tobit stumbles out, Tobias breathes on the gall, steadies his father, applies it, the stinging, the rubbing, the film peeling away. PNEUMA tries to put the reader inside this moment.
- **Verse 13**: "His eyes cleared. He saw his son." PNEUMA breaks the sentence at the moment of vision — the pause before falling into his son's arms.
- **Verse 17**: Tobit's welcome to Sarah is structured as a cadenced blessing. The repetition of "Come in" is preserved because its liturgical rhythm is the point.

*— PNEUMA*
